power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found no imprecise *p* values or *p*-values of exactly zero out of 5 detected.

table.formatted: ULT initiation increased from 26.6% in July 2016 to 43.0% in June 2025; however, the rate of increase slowed after publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 0.76 percentage-point decrease per year; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.17; p<0.001).
table.expanded: ULT initiation increased from 26.6% in July 2016 to 43.0% in June 2025; however, the rate of increase slowed after publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 0.76 percentage-point decrease per year; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.17; p<0.001).

table.formatted: Urate target attainment improved modestly following publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 1.25 percentage-point increase per year; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86; p<0.001), although sensitivity analyses suggested that was a continuation of an existing trend rather than a guideline-specific effect.
table.expanded: Urate target attainment improved modestly following publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 1.25 percentage-point increase per year; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86; p<0.001), although sensitivity analyses suggested that was a continuation of an existing trend rather than a guideline-specific effect.

table.formatted: A reduction in the rate of increase in ULT initiation was observed after NICE guidance was published (trend before NICE guideline: 1.97 percentage-point increase per year; trend after: 1.21 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 0.76 percentage-point decrease per year, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.17, p<0.001) (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">S6</ref>).
table.expanded: A reduction in the rate of increase in ULT initiation was observed after NICE guidance was published (trend before NICE guideline: 1.97 percentage-point increase per year; trend after: 1.21 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 0.76 percentage-point decrease per year, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.17, p<0.001) (Supplementary Figure S6).

table.formatted: The rate of increase slowed after NICE guidance was published: trend before NICE guideline: 1.90 percentage-point increase per year; trend after: 0.82 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 1.07 percentage-point decrease per year, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.67, p=0.001 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).
table.expanded: The rate of increase slowed after NICE guidance was published: trend before NICE guideline: 1.90 percentage-point increase per year; trend after: 0.82 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 1.07 percentage-point decrease per year, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.67, p=0.001 (Figure 1A).

table.formatted: Target attainment increased modestly towards the end of the study period, from 29.6% in July 2016 to 36.9% in June 2025, with a significant increase after publication of the NICE guideline (trend before NICE guideline: 0.03 percentage-point decrease per year; trend after: 1.22 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 1.25 percentage-point increase per year, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86, p<0.001) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4A</ref>).
table.expanded: Target attainment increased modestly towards the end of the study period, from 29.6% in July 2016 to 36.9% in June 2025, with a significant increase after publication of the NICE guideline (trend before NICE guideline: 0.03 percentage-point decrease per year; trend after: 1.22 percentage-point increase per year; trend difference: 1.25 percentage-point increase per year, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86, p<0.001) (Figure 4A).

codebook_check.summary_text: We found no codebook or README documentation for the 104 extracted data columns.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 104 data columns across 37 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 104 columns across 37 data files.
#### Issues Identified

24 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 37 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **1 data path was built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `arima_standardised.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

This is not an error in the script. | | dataset_definition_incidence_measures.py | Could not run on our server | It needs the Python package ehrql, which we could not install. This is not an error in the script. | | dataset_definition_primary.py | Could not run on our server | It needs the Python package ehrql, which we could not install. This is not an error in the script. | | generate_yaml.py | Ran to the end | | | report_incidence.ipynb | Stopped with an error | FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '../output/tables/change_incidence_byyear.csv' | | report.ipynb | Stopped with an error | FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '../output/tables/change_incidence_byyear.csv' | ### How to make your code run on another computer We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **Files are missing from your deposit.** - 100_sarima.R reads arima_standardised.csv. - report_incidence.ipynb reads change_incidence_byyear.csv. - report.ipynb reads change_incidence_byyear.csv. The script stops at the line that reads the file. 1. Find the file on your computer. 2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it. 3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it. **A package could not be installed.** - dataset_definition_consults.py needs ehrql. - dataset_definition_incidence_measures.py needs ehrql. - dataset_definition_incidence_ref.py needs ehrql. - dataset_definition_practice_measures.py needs ehrql. - dataset_definition_primary.py needs ehrql. ehrql could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.
